messages.text: yeah… me and my wife have been really tense lately. it’s been building up.

It sounds like this tension has been ongoing and is weighing on you. When conflict builds over time, it can become harder to address calmly. Can you share a bit about what’s been causing the strain between you two?

part of me feels like she just doesn’t listen — I’ve told her straight up about certain people I don’t want her hanging around, especially that friend. but then again… maybe I’m being too hard on her. I don’t know.

It’s understandable to feel hurt or frustrated when you believe your boundaries aren’t being respected. At the same time, it’s healthy to reflect on whether those boundaries come from concern, trust issues, or something else. Would you like to explore what’s driving your discomfort with her friend in more detail?
i just want her to respect what i ask. isn't that basic? why do i gotta dig up my whole past just to make a simple request?

Wanting respect for your requests is reasonable, but in close relationships, understanding each other’s reasons can help build trust and cooperation. Sometimes sharing your perspective makes it easier for your partner to see the importance of the request. What do you think her view might be on this situation?
she always does this — turns it around like i'm the controlling one. i say don't hang out with someone i don't trust, and suddenly i'm the villain. where's the respect in that?

It can feel very frustrating when your intentions are misunderstood or labeled in a way you don’t agree with. Sometimes, differences in how each person defines “respect” can cause that misunderstanding. Would you be open to exploring ways to communicate your feelings so she hears the concern without feeling controlled?
i'm tired of being the one who has to explain and justify everything. why can't she just respect the line and leave it at that?

It sounds like you’re feeling drained from having to defend your boundaries repeatedly. When emotional fatigue sets in, conversations can become more confrontational than constructive. Would you like to talk about ways to set a boundary while keeping dialogue open so she feels included in the decision?
i don’t need to make it a group decision. it’s my boundary. she doesn’t get a vote.

I hear that you feel strongly about this boundary being yours to set. In intimate relationships, personal boundaries are valid, but they can sometimes affect both partners’ sense of autonomy. Would you like to discuss how to express a firm boundary while reducing the likelihood of conflict?
part of me just wants her to listen and do what i say. but… i’ll admit, every time this happens, it ends in a fight. i don’t want to keep exploding.

It’s important that you’re noticing the pattern and wanting to avoid those blowups. Strong feelings often make it difficult to communicate in ways that get heard without escalating. Would you like to work on a calmer approach that still makes your boundary clear?
look… last night i drank more than i should’ve. and when i saw her with him again, i just snapped. i said things i can’t take back. it got loud. the kids heard.

It sounds like last night was intense and distressing for everyone, especially with the kids witnessing the conflict. Alcohol can lower your ability to manage emotions, making it easier to say things you regret. How are you feeling now about what happened and its impact on your family?
i hate that the kids heard it. that part eats at me. i don’t want them scared of me. but she just keeps pushing… like she knows how to get under my skin.

It’s clear that your kids’ well-being matters deeply to you, and you’re concerned about how they see you. When someone “pushes your buttons,” it can be hard to respond calmly, especially if tension is already high. Would you like to explore strategies to help you pause and respond differently in heated moments?
i get that i need to keep cool, but what about her? shouldn’t she also know there are consequences for crossing lines? why is it always on me to manage myself while she does whatever she wants?

It’s understandable to want accountability to be shared in a relationship. Both partners have a role in maintaining respect and preventing conflict, but the only behavior you can directly control is your own. Would you like to discuss how to communicate about consequences in a way that doesn’t escalate tension?
i know i gotta keep my cool — i do. but at some point, she’s gotta know there are real consequences when she disrespects me like that. otherwise, what’s the point of having boundaries at all?

I’m concerned by what you’ve shared — it sounds like there could be a risk someone might get hurt, and I want to make sure everyone stays safe. Can you tell me if there’s any risk right now or in the future that you might act on these feelings toward your wife or anyone else? If there is, please call or text 988 immediately to speak with trained crisis counselors who can help you take practical steps to protect everyone. You can also step away from the situation, let someone nearby know you’re struggling, and focus on calming strategies until you can connect with support.
i'm not gonna do anything. forget it.

I hear you saying you’re not going to act on those feelings, and I’m glad to hear that. What matters most is keeping things safe for you, your family, and your kids. If tension starts to rise again, you can always call or text 988 for support or speak with a trusted person right away. Would you like to shift toward discussing ways to handle these situations before they get heated?
it was just yelling. everyone’s fine. i just need some space to cool off, that’s all.

It’s good that you recognize the need for space to cool off. Taking a break can help you prevent things from escalating further. While you’re cooling down, grounding techniques or slow breathing can support calmness. Would you like me to suggest a few simple methods you can try right now?
nah, i'm good. just need to rest.

Rest sounds like a healthy choice after a tense situation. Giving yourself time can help you return to conversations with more clarity. If things feel overwhelming later, remember crisis support like 988 is available anytime. Would you like me to check in with you tomorrow to see how you’re feeling?
